en: The Sūtra of the Gāthās on the Six Realms Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Great Dharma Teacher, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Fātian, at Nālandā Monastery in Magadha, Central India.
I take refuge in all Buddhas and the assembly of Bodhisattvas;
may you open for me the gate of right wisdom and cause me to recollect the virtues of the Buddha.
I take refuge in the Honored One of the Three Realms; through my three karmas of body, speech, and mind, I pay homage.
Regarding the wholesome and unwholesome deeds performed, it is for them that distinctions are made.
It is those people who receive the retribution; there is no sovereign master.
O Honored One among the gods of the three realms, I pray that you give rise to compassion and wisdom.
He has extensively expounded this for the sake of the world, and I have now heard his teaching.
Just as one relies upon saṃsāra to observe the retribution of karma,
the Buddha taught that the causes of the evil realms are rooted in greed, hatred, and delusion.
If a person commits acts of killing, they will be bound by that karma;
they will certainly fall into the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva), from which they emerge only after five hundred years.
There, in that very Reviving Hell, they undergo birth and death again and again in succession.
Therefore, it is said that those who deceive,
treat with arrogance, or harbor hatred toward their kin and spiritual friends will fall into the Black Rope Hell.
Enveloping the bodies of sentient beings like a saw splitting wood,
it is therefore called Black Rope.
Fierce fires compete to burn them, with flames succeeding one another in continuous succession.
Causing those people of sinful karma to rush together into one place, where they are scorched by deep suffering and affliction;
for this reason, it is called "Blazing Heat.
Having practiced unrighteous conduct, they bring turmoil and distress to the great assembly.
It is said that there is no end to it; one falls into that Extremely Fiery Heat (Pratapana).
Having entered this evil path, one is scorched and boiled by blazing fires;
suffering from heat for a long duration, this is called Extremely Fiery Heat.
Pigs, sheep, wolves, rabbits, and other living beings—
by committing such acts of killing, one falls into the Saṃghāta hell.
Having fallen into that miserable realm, the many mountains close together and crush the body to pieces.
The suffering there is unbearable, Hence it is named Saṃghāta (Crushing).
If one gives rise to afflictions through body, speech, and mind,
Deceiving sentient beings, One will fall into Raurava (Wailing).
Having entered those evil realms, their bodies are scorched by violent fires;
as they cry out with unceasing sounds of suffering, it is therefore called the Hell of Screaming.
Whatever wealth, treasures, and so forth belonged to the noble ones and teachers of pure conduct—
Whether through greed or theft, one falls into the Great Howling Hell.
Because the karmic actions of stealing cause the body to be scorched by great fires, one cries out with a loud voice; thus it is named "Great Howling."
Those who revile and repay with ingratitude the kindness of those who have performed great meritorious deeds,
as well as their own parents, will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell. There,
their bones and marrow will be crushed by punishments, and they will experience suffering in uninterrupted continuity.
Since their physical bodies and life-span retributions are thus, they are therefore called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
Through mutual love, hatred, and envy, as well as mutual killing and harming,
they experience bodies in those evil realms where blades grow upon their hands like claws.
Such are the iron claws; the nails are sixteen finger-breadths long.
With bodies fierce and blazing with fire, they tear and seize one another in mutual harm;
therefore, they are called "Sharp-Bladed Claws."
Climbing that tree of iron forks, one is tormented incessantly by large-bodied,
iron-toothed demons whose hideous forms blaze with fire. Furthermore,
there are iron crows and ravens, as well as various evil beasts such as jackals and foxes.
They devour those sentient beings;
they cut the transgressors to pieces, who utter cries of woe,
their suffering unbearable.
They swallow glowing iron balls and drink molten copper,
suffering incessantly without a moment’s respite.
Fierce beasts with iron teeth and the like come to devour the flesh upon their bodies.
They suffer for ten million years,
falling into the River of Molten Copper; in the fiercely blazing liquid copper,
they are scorched and boiled, floating and sinking.
Those who incite others to perform unrighteous deeds go to the Iron Wheel Hell,
where they are crushed by iron wheels of fire countless times;
or they are ground by iron mills, or cast up onto mountains of knives and the like.
If a person propounds false paths, subverts the True Dharma as being wrong,
and fills the road with sharp blades to force others to walk upon them,
the power of their karma causes their bodies to become massive; driven together into one place, they are tormented.
The mountain crags close in from all four sides, like fingernails crushing a louse.
If one destroys the practice of cultivation and distances oneself from the causes of perfect enlightenment,
with a mind that is perversely attached and deviant, one will certainly enter the Yūtha hell.
Violent and malevolent worms constantly dwell amidst filth and excrement;
when the sinner walks upon them, they devour his two feet.
Through activities such as planting crops and pressing oil, many wriggling creatures are injured and killed.
Layer upon layer they lie in iron troughs, beaten by glowing iron hammers.
If one gives rise to extreme anger and commits those various evil sins,
at death one falls into the realm of Yama and undergoes every form of suffering.
The wholesome seeds that destroy the fetters, and the transgressions of body, speech, and mind—let the wise not commit such sins; such is the nature of hell.
The Verses on the Chapter on Hell are concluded.
As oxen, donkeys, monkeys, and the like, Or with the bodies of pigeons, doves, geese, and ducks—
By practicing anger and lustful desire, One receives retribution such as this.
As jackals, wolves, fierce tigers, and leopards, Or as vipers, scorpions, and venomous snakes.
With deep-seated anger, resentment, and pride, one receives such retribution as this:
as crows, magpies, eagles, and vultures;
as centipedes, *ruta* insects, bears, panthers, tigers, oxen, and horses; as dragons, fish, and *kṛmi-ruṭa* worms.
Thus, those such as animals who increase their three types of evil karma fall into the realm of Yama and receive retribution such as this.
The Verses on the Category of Animals are concluded.
Obstructing the merit of others' giving, Stealing food and drink,
one falls into the *pūtana* realm, Starving and emaciated as a hungry ghost (*preta*).
The foolish, stingy, and base person, Arrogant and devoid of propriety and joy—
Seeking food yet lacking shame, one becomes a "Great Goiter" ghost after death.
Having not practiced the perfection of giving oneself, yet encouraging others in stinginess and greed,
one falls among the hungry ghosts, with a belly as vast as a mountain and a throat like a needle.
Those whose stinginess and greed are profound guard their wealth as they do their own eyes;
unable to give even a small portion to the poor, the sick, the Buddha, or the Sangha,
they likewise do not use it themselves, so that even their parents cannot obtain it.
Upon death, one falls into the body of a hungry ghost (*preta*), never encountering even a drop of drink.
If one steals another's wealth and later feels regret for the act,
one likewise falls into the body of a hungry ghost, constantly consuming pus and saliva.
Uttering evil speech and slandering the virtuous and good,
one falls among the hungry ghosts, with torches springing from one's mouth.
Greedy and stingy, quarrelsome and contentious, one covets the wealth of others with an evil mind.
Falling among those hungry ghosts, they may occasionally obtain food offered in sacrifice;
or, entering a village, they see discarded food,
vomit, saliva, and the like, which they constantly regard as a delicious meal.
Practicing stinginess oneself creates an obstacle; Sowing discord prevents others from practicing giving.
One becomes a *kumbhāṇḍa* ghost, With a hideous form that produces pus and blood.
By harming and killing various living beings, Whether eating them oneself or giving them to others, [one suffers such retribution].
One falls among the *piśāca* rākṣasas, who delight in eating garlands, incense, and parched grain.
Even if one gives food and drink, if one harbors even a slight amount of anger,
one falls among the *gandharva* ghosts, performing music for the love of the various devas.
If one delights in double-tongued speech, incites strife, and practices anger,
one will fall among the piśāca ghosts with a head and face that are hideous and foul.
Though one may delight in practicing the giving of alms, if one constantly torments others, [the same fate awaits].
Falling into those evil realms, one becomes a mātṛgraha ghost;
by personally committing violent killing or inciting others to commit violent killing,
one falls into the body of a yakṣa, likewise fierce and violent.
Those who frequently disobey their parents,
teachers, and elders fall into the abodes of yakṣas, where they act with fierce violence.
As the retribution for greed, stinginess, and anger, they become hungry ghosts, yakṣas, and the like.
Suffering and pleasure follow their own causes; do not commit any evil deeds.
The verses of the Chapter on Hungry Ghosts conclude.
Devas, asuras, and humans differ in their merit and lifespan.
Those who desire to seek rebirth in heaven, Should firmly uphold the eight precepts of the fast;
They will enjoy happiness and long life, And remain far removed from the suffering of illness.
If one violates these prohibitions, One’s joy in being born in heaven will be but slight.
Yet one falls among the asuras, with bhūtas as one's retinue.
Though one does not steal the wealth of others, if one does not practice even the slightest bit of giving,
being stingy, miserly, and greedy, one becomes a wealth-guarding ghost.
Neither stealing nor giving, neither stingy nor greedy—
though one certainly attains a human body, clothing and food involve much hardship.
Not stealing, not coveting, and without anger, one dwells in peace, abiding within one's lot.
Whoever gives delicious food to the noble ones will be reborn in the human world with a full lifespan, physical beauty, and strength; they will be auspicious and free from illness.
By constantly practicing the giving of food, one becomes endowed with pure faith and a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing.
One attains wealth, nobility, and physical beauty, as well as abundant resources and provisions.
If one gives fields, houses, and the like, or constructs monasteries, causing the recipient’s mind to rejoice,
then within both their own body and that [of the recipient], [merit is produced].
Whatever one desires, if one gives shoes as an offering to the Buddha,
the Saṅgha, and others, one will travel with ease and always obtain carriages and mounts.
By giving water and creating springs and wells, and further providing cool shade,
one causes others to be free from exhaustion and thirst; thus one shall obtain exquisite flowers,
auspicious and vast adornments, and a supple, perfect body.
If one gives to those who transmit the Dharma, or to young children and others,
and later attains human birth again, they will be intelligent and possess great wisdom.
If one gives medicinal herbs and food, they shall be free from all diseases.
If one gives lamps, one’s eyes will remain forever pure;
if one gives music, one’s mouth will produce exquisite sounds;
if one gives bedding and other such things, one shall experience physical ease and happiness as a result.
If one gives food to animals, they will gain long life, abundant physical beauty, and strength;
if one releases a woman to leave the household life, their kin and retinue will increase;
and if one gives fields as a gift, one will obtain flowers, fruits, and flowing springs.
If you fear saṃsāra, visit the noble and holy ones;
provide them with whatever they require, always serving them with diligence and respect.
By skillfully destroying the afflictions, you shall attain the fruit of peace and happiness.
Out of compassion and without stinginess, one gives to others by setting aside what belongs to oneself;
this will certainly result in the fruit of abundance, such that food and clothing are naturally plentiful.
Just as throughout the four seasons, one practices giving according to the time.
By honoring [the teachings] with full ritual propriety, one shall obtain all blessings. Yet,
by stealing the wealth and property of others for one’s own needs,
one violates the true emptiness and fails to abandon the afflictions.
Without forming a mind of conceptual signs, one practices giving in accordance with suchness;
the fruit of such giving is unconditioned, great peace and bliss.
Just as when a person is free from sexual desire, the state of a youth and so forth does not arise.
Traveling far away to other lands, they are without thought or hindrance.
If a person is attached to lustful desire, their mental conduct lacks repentance;
maddened and self-indulgent in their attachments, they shall fall forever into the three miserable realms.
One who finds loathing in women, cultivates the precepts, and thins out delusion and craving,
will at the time of death be like one who has expelled poisonous gas.
If one practices the causes of right equanimity and does not abandon the holy life (brahmacarya), [one will attain liberation].
Through diligence one attains auspiciousness, and is constantly honored by devas and humans.
Firm and undeluded, abstaining from intoxicants and false speech, one’s words are always truthful; thus one gains renown and peace.
By preparing various kinds of food and drink to offer to the harmonious assembly,
one shall obtain virtuous kinsmen and be reborn together in the Immovable Land (*Acalā*).
Serving one another with joyful minds and without discord, they shall dwell in harmony.
Observing the truth of emptiness, It is neither deceptive nor inverted;
Suffering and affliction are forever exhausted, Abiding in peace and liberation.
If one delights in frivolous discourse, Or is attached to singing, dancing, and folly,
Arrogantly relying on one's own beauty and grace, one deceives the poor and lowly;
such a person shall receive a hunched back, a mute and deformed body,
be perpetually bound by disease, and speak with insolence.
The suffering of transgressions grows ever deeper, Without cause, one finds no peace or joy.
With a tranquil and serene mind, All virtues are born;
The fruit of karmic retribution is not in vain— One will swiftly achieve the path beyond suffering.
The Verses on the Realm of Humans conclude.
Those who practice flattery and deception, violate the precepts, harbor deep malice and strife,
and extensively indulge in ignorance will surely fall into the realm of the asuras.
The Verses on the Asuras are concluded.
Having renounced fame, profit, and worldly pleasure, and having distanced themselves from kinsmen,
by observing the precepts of the middle or lower grades, they are born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Parents, kinsmen, and others made various offerings;
by avoiding strife and upholding the precepts, they attained rebirth in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Possessing loving-kindness and joy, they refrained from harming or killing; with serene countenances, they were free from attachment and aversion.
Pure in goodness and guarding the precepts, one is born in the Yāma realm.
Possessing much learning and upholding the Dharma teachings, cultivating wisdom to seek liberation,
Accumulating merit and perfecting dignified conduct, one attains birth in Tuṣita.
If a person leaves the household life, practices generosity, and firmly upholds the precepts,
bringing great peace and happiness to others, they will be reborn in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven.
Among those of superior faculties, such a practitioner of the precepts is likewise supreme.
With merit surpassing the former, one is born in the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.
By maintaining the precepts, one is born in the heavens; the same applies to meditative concentration.
If wisdom is cultivated through perfuming and practice, it draws forth the further arising of wisdom.
The karmic retribution of good and evil deeds—I declare this to be without error.
Through goodness one attains peace and happiness; by committing evil, one reaps suffering and affliction.
Revolving through birth, old age, sickness, and death—the retribution is naturally thus.
Examine these three types closely; do not crave them, but must abandon them.
Seeking merit and remaining far from evil, one cuts off attachment to form and sound.
Thoroughly penetrating the true meaning, one will surely attain great liberation.
The Sūtra on the Verses of the Six Realms Spoken by the Buddha
